title: The Ghost Case
hook: He killed a ghost. The High Court believed him.

status.explain: Section 79 IPC (now BNS §17) continues to protect bona fide acts committed under genuine mistake of fact where due care is evaluated relative to the accused's circumstances.

episodes.title: A HAUNTED AIRSTRIP IN THE MAYURBHANJ JUNGLE.

blocks.text: In May 1958, an abandoned World War II military aerodrome at Rasgovindpur in Mayurbhanj district lay engulfed by dense Sal forests. Jagat Bandhu Chatterjee (PW 1), a Calcutta scrap merchant, had arrived with his Nepali servant Ram Bahadur Thapa to collect discarded aerodrome metal scrap. The local tribal villagers warned them persistently that the abandoned runway was haunted by malevolent ghosts who roamed after midnight and killed trespassers.

LEGAL ANALYSIS: This opening episode establishes the physical environment and subjective state of mind of the accused. In criminal law, liability for homicide under IPC §302 requires mens rea (guilty intention or knowledge); the surrounding atmosphere of supernatural terror becomes critical to assessing whether the subsequent acts were committed under a bona fide mistake of fact under Section 79 IPC.

student.ratio: An act done under a bona fide mistake of fact, believing in good faith that one is attacking an evil spirit and not a human being, is protected under Section 79 IPC.

blocks.text: TRIAL PROPOSITION: Atmospheric evidence establishing deep-rooted local belief in supernatural spirits and absence of prior animus is admissible to substantiate a bona fide mistake of fact under Section 79 IPC.

pinpoints.proposition: Atmospheric terror and absence of prior grudge are critical baseline factors for Section 79.

episodes.endHook: How did the midnight inspection turn tragic? Continue to Episode 2 ↓

episodes.title: THE SCRAP DEALER, THE SERVANT, AND THE VILLAGERS.

blocks.text:
PERSONA 01 — RESPONDENT (ACCUSED)
Ram Bahadur Thapa
A 20-year-old Nepali domestic servant in the employ of Chatterjee, completely unacquainted with the local Santali language and steeped in belief in spirits.

PERSONA 02 — CHIEF PROSECUTION WITNESS (PW 1)
Jagat Bandhu Chatterjee
Calcutta scrap dealer whose firm bought aerodrome scrap and who led the midnight venture.

PERSONA 03 — LANDLORD WITNESS (PW 2)
Chandra Majhi
Local landlord at whose house Chatterjee lodged and who reinforced the haunting lore.

PERSONA 04 — THE VICTIMS
Gelhi Majhiani (deceased), Ganga Majhiani, and Dukhi Majhiani
Tribal Majhi women who ventured onto the airstrip with a hurricane lamp to gather fallen Mohua flowers.

LEGAL ANALYSIS: Note the demographic background of Thapa — a simple Nepali youth in an alien territory who had never met the victims. The total absence of prior acquaintance or motive is the indispensable evidentiary pillar proving that the fatal assault was not premeditated murder.

student.ratio: The absence of any previous grudge, motive, or acquaintance between the accused and the victim supports the inference of an honest mistake of fact rather than intentional homicide.
student.examAngle: Exam focus: Distinction between Motive, Intention, and Knowledge in Indian Criminal Law.

blocks.text: TRIAL PROPOSITION: Establishing absolute absence of prior acquaintance, motive, or ill-will between accused and victim is an indispensable prerequisite to sustain an unassailable Section 79 defence.

pinpoints.proposition: Total absence of motive negates malicious intent under Section 300 IPC.

episodes.endHook: What happened on the stormy midnight of May 20? Continue to Episode 3 ↓

episodes.title: A FLICKERING LIGHT IN A MIDNIGHT STORM.

blocks.text: On the dark, stormy midnight of 20 May 1958, around 11:30 PM, Chatterjee and Thapa set out with landlord Chandra Majhi to inspect the aerodrome. Drizzling rain and heavy wind swept across the runway. Suddenly, deep within the Sal grove, they spotted a flickering, swinging light bobbing up and down in the pitch darkness. Chandra Majhi immediately exclaimed that it was the ghost. In a state of sudden terror, Ram Bahadur Thapa rushed towards the flickering light shouting 'Ghost! Ghost!' and brandished his khukri to strike at the apparition.

source.paraText: The party saw a flickering light in the aerodrome and thought it was a ghost.

blocks.text: LEGAL ANALYSIS: This episode contains the critical factual trigger — the flickering light in complete darkness during a squall, accompanied by the companion's contemporaneous shout of 'Ghost!'. Under Section 6 Evidence Act (Res Gestae), spontaneous contemporaneous reactions form part of the same transaction and establish the accused's bona fide perception.

student.ratio: Contemporaneous declarations and atmospheric cues at the scene of the incident are admissible to prove the accused's genuine perception of a supernatural threat.
student.examAngle: Relevance under Section 6 Indian Evidence Act (Res Gestae) and Section 79 IPC.

blocks.text: TRIAL PROPOSITION: Spontaneous contemporaneous declarations of companions ('Ghost! Ghost!') form part of the res gestae and substantiate the accused's genuine subjective belief under Section 79.

source.paraText: Res gestae and contemporaneous terror under Section 6 Evidence Act.

pinpoints.proposition: Contemporaneous cry of companions establishes the factual context of terror.

episodes.endHook: What lay behind the flickering light? Continue to Episode 4 ↓

episodes.title: THE MOHUA GATHERERS IN THE DARK.

blocks.text: The flickering light was not a ghost. It was a small hurricane lantern brought by a party of tribal Santali women who had sheltered under a Mohua tree to collect fallen flowers. In the darkness and raging wind, Thapa indiscriminately swung his khukri at what he believed to be an evil spirit. Gelhi Majhiani received fatal wounds and died on the spot; Ganga Majhiani and Dukhi Majhiani sustained severe injuries. When Chatterjee ran up with his torch and shone it on the scene, Thapa froze in horror upon realizing he had struck human beings.

source.paraText: The light was from a lantern carried by tribal women gathering Mohua flowers.

blocks.text: LEGAL ANALYSIS: The distinction between the objective reality (human beings collecting flowers) and the subjective reality of the accused (evil spirits roaming the runway) is the classical matrix for *Ignorantia facti excusat*. Had the facts been as Thapa genuinely believed them to be (an attack against a deadly ghost), his act would have been lawful and justified in self-defence/community protection.

source.paraText: Objective facts vs. subjective belief of the accused.

student.ratio: Under Section 79 IPC, the culpability of the accused must be judged on the assumption that the mistaken state of facts honestly believed by him was the true state of affairs.
student.examAngle: The classic Latin maxim: Ignorantia facti excusat, ignorantia juris non excusat.

blocks.text: TRIAL PROPOSITION: In evaluating Section 79, the court must test criminal culpability by placing the accused in the position of the facts as he honestly and mistakenly believed them to exist.

source.paraText: The hypothetical test under Section 79: judging acts as if the mistaken facts were true.

pinpoints.proposition: The act must be evaluated as if the mistaken facts were real.

episodes.endHook: How did the Sessions Court decide the charge of murder? Continue to Episode 5 ↓

episodes.title: MURDER (IPC 302) VS. MISTAKE OF FACT (IPC 79).

blocks.text:
The State charged Ram Bahadur Thapa under Section 302 IPC for the murder of Gelhi Majhiani, Section 326 IPC for grievous hurt to Ganga Majhiani, and Section 324 IPC for hurt to Dukhi Majhiani.

THE PROSECUTION ARGUED:
Thapa acted with reckless negligence. Striking indiscriminately with a lethal khukri in pitch darkness without verifying the identity of the figures showed a gross lack of 'due care and attention' under Section 52 IPC, forfeiting the protection of Section 79.

THE DEFENCE ARGUED:
Thapa acted under genuine, overwhelming terror in an isolated haunted jungle. He had no malice, no motive, and honestly believed he was attacking a ghost threatening his master's party. The Sessions Judge of Mayurbhanj accepted the defence and acquitted Thapa on all counts.

source.paraText: Trial and acquittal by the Sessions Judge under Section 79 IPC.

blocks.text: LEGAL ANALYSIS: The core legal confrontation centers on the interpretation of 'Good Faith' under Section 52 IPC. The prosecution contended for an objective, ideal standard of prudent conduct, whereas the defence maintained that due care must be interpreted in light of the accused's background, education, terror, and physical environment.

source.paraText: Interpretation of Section 52 IPC good faith threshold.

student.ratio: Section 52 IPC 'due care and attention' does not mandate superhuman prudence, but the care expected of a reasonable person in the accused's specific situation and state of mind.
student.examAngle: Definition of 'Good Faith' under Section 52 IPC versus Section 3(22) General Clauses Act.

blocks.text: TRIAL PROPOSITION: The requirement of 'due care and attention' under Section 52 IPC is relative, not absolute, and must be judged from the standpoint of the accused in his specific psychological and physical circumstances.

source.paraText: Relative standard of due care and attention under Section 52.

pinpoints.proposition: Good faith under Section 52 is relative to the accused's circumstances and mental state.

episodes.endHook: How did the High Court rule on the State's appeal against acquittal? Continue to Episode 6 ↓

episodes.title: CAN A BELIEF IN GHOSTS JUSTIFY HOMICIDE IN LAW?

blocks.text:
A woman has lost her life, and two others are gravely wounded. The killer admits wielding the khukri, but swears he believed with all his heart that he was defending against a demonic phantom.

Two contrasting legal positions stood before the High Court:

> THE STRICT LIABILITY DOCTRINE: Criminal law cannot countenance superstition as an excuse for killing human beings; convict for culpable homicide.

> THE GENERAL EXCEPTION SHIELD: Criminal law punishes the guilty mind (mens rea); an honest subjective mistake of fact negates guilt; dismiss the State's appeal.

source.paraText: The legal dilemma before the Division Bench.

blocks.text: LEGAL ANALYSIS: The judicial question before Chief Justice Narasimham was whether criminal law requires strict objective rationality or whether it accommodates the subjective realities of simple citizens acting under sudden fright without malice.

source.paraText: Subjective test of mens rea vs objective rationality.

student.ratio: Criminal liability requires subjective moral blameworthiness; an honest mistake of fact eliminates the mens rea necessary for criminal conviction.
student.examAngle: Exam question: Can superstitious belief constitute a valid defence under Section 79 IPC?

blocks.text: TRIAL PROPOSITION: Where subjective panic and honest mistake of fact eliminate conscious criminal intent, the general exception of Section 79 IPC overrides the prima facie offence of homicide.

source.paraText: Section 79 overrides homicide when mens rea is absent due to mistake of fact.

pinpoints.proposition: Absence of mens rea due to mistake of fact excludes liability for homicide.

episodes.endHook: How did Chief Justice Narasimham deliver the landmark ruling? Continue to Episode 7 ↓

episodes.title: THE HIGH COURT AFFIRMS THE ACQUITTAL.

blocks.text:
The Division Bench of the Orissa High Court, headed by Chief Justice R.L. Narasimham and Justice S. Barman, dismissed the State's appeal and affirmed the acquittal of Ram Bahadur Thapa on all charges.

Chief Justice Narasimham held that Thapa was completely unacquainted with the area, had no motive or grudge against the victims, and was gripped by intense terror induced by the surrounding atmosphere and his landlord's shouts. The Court ruled that 'due care and attention' under Section 52 IPC must be evaluated considering the mental state, fear, and intellectual capacity of the accused. Since Thapa honestly believed he was attacking a ghost, his act was protected under Section 79 IPC as an act done under a bona fide mistake of fact.

source.paraText: The High Court dismissed the appeal and upheld the acquittal under Section 79 IPC.

blocks.text: LEGAL ANALYSIS: Memorize the binding holding: The High Court held that the standard of due care and attention under Section 52 is not fixed or mechanical. In conditions of pitch darkness, rain, howling wind, and pervasive superstition, an impulsive attack on an apparition does not amount to culpable rashness or murder.

source.paraText: Operative holding on Section 52 and Section 79 IPC.

student.ratio: A person who, under a bona fide mistake of fact caused by atmospheric terror and superstition, attacks human beings believing them to be evil spirits, is protected by Section 79 IPC and entitled to full acquittal.
student.examAngle: Key Precedents Affirmed: Waryam Singh v. Emperor (AIR 1926 Lah 554) and Bonda Kui v. Emperor (AIR 1943 Pat 64).

blocks.text: TRIAL PROPOSITION: The High Court confirmed that Section 79 IPC provides complete immunity from conviction under Sections 302, 326, and 324 IPC where the act is committed under a bona fide mistake of fact without malice.

source.paraText: High Court's confirmation of full acquittal under Section 79 IPC.

pinpoints.proposition: Section 79 IPC operates as a complete defense to charges of murder and grievous hurt.

episodes.title: IGNORANTIA FACTI EXCUSAT: THE LIMITS OF CRIMINAL CULPABILITY.

blocks.text:
State of Orissa v. Ram Bahadur Thapa stands as India's foremost authority on the criminal law defense of mistake of fact under Section 79 IPC (now Section 17 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023).

The judgment firmly entrenched the principle that criminal guilt requires conscious blameworthiness. It established that 'good faith' does not require infallible wisdom or superhuman presence of mind in moments of sudden terror, and that the courts must judge the legality of an act based upon the facts as the accused honestly perceived them.

source.paraText: Doctrinal legacy and statutory transition to BNS §17.

blocks.text: LEGAL ANALYSIS: When writing exam answers on Criminal Law General Exceptions: Cite this case for the subjective standard of Section 52 ('Good Faith') and the absolute excusing power of Section 79 ('Mistake of Fact'). Note the statutory transition from IPC §79 to Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS) §17.

source.paraText: Summary of doctrinal rules for academic analysis.

student.ratio: Section 79 IPC / BNS §17 protects bona fide acts committed under an honest mistake of fact; due care and attention under Section 52 is contextual and subjective.
student.examAngle: Provisions: IPC §79 (now BNS §17), IPC §52 (now BNS §2(11)), Evidence Act §105 (burden of proof on general exceptions).

blocks.text: TRIAL PROPOSITION: Section 79 IPC (BNS §17) establishes that mistake of fact excuses criminal liability when the accused acts in good faith according to his honest perception of the facts.

source.paraText: The general proposition on mistake of fact under Indian criminal jurisprudence.

pinpoints.proposition: Mistake of fact excuses criminal liability when acted upon in good faith under Section 79.

statutoryText.quotedText: "79. Act done by a person justified, or by mistake of fact believing himself justified, by law.—Nothing is an offence which is done by any person who is justified by law, or who by reason of a mistake of fact and not by reason of a mistake of law in good faith believes himself to be justified by law, in doing it."
"52. 'Good faith'.—Nothing is said to be done or believed in 'good faith' which is done or believed without due care and attention."

holdings.holding: An accused who attacks human beings under a bona fide belief that he is attacking an evil spirit or ghost is protected under Section 79 IPC by reason of a mistake of fact.

The standard of 'due care and attention' under Section 52 IPC is not an absolute or uniform standard; it must be assessed having regard to the intelligence, social background, surrounding atmosphere of terror, and immediate physical circumstances of the accused.
The absence of previous grudge, motive, or prior acquaintance between the accused and the victim strongly supports the inference of an honest mistake of fact under Section 79.
Under Section 79 IPC, the criminality of an act must be judged on the assumption that the mistaken state of facts honestly believed by the accused was the true state of affairs.
The High Court confirmed that Section 79 IPC provides complete immunity from conviction under Sections 302, 326, and 324 IPC where mens rea is negated by honest mistake of fact.

precedents.proposition: Accused who assaulted a nocturnal trespasser in the bona fide belief that he was a ghost held entitled to the protection of Section 79 IPC.
A woman who killed an intruder in pitch darkness believing it to be an evil spirit was acquitted under Section 79 IPC.
On the construction of 'due care and attention' under Section 52 IPC as being relative to the person and the circumstances.
On subjective perception, terror, and sudden impulse negating deliberate malice in criminal law.

affectsYou.heading: Why The Ghost Case precedent protects rights today
points: Protects individuals from murder charges when an honest, reasonable mistake of fact removes all criminal intention.
Establishes that courts must consider human fear, terror, and contextual panic rather than applying abstract mechanical standards.
Forms the foundation for modern criminal jurisprudence on general exceptions under Section 17 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
